angle: When a museum strips out all wall text and calls itself 'open to interpretation', does context actually disappear for everyone equally — the first gallery where a deaf visitor stands on level ground — or does the information never vanish at all, just migrate into speech, docents, and murmured conversation, rebuilding the old hierarchy in the one channel I can't audit?
correction_moment: At Calder Gardens in Philadelphia in October, arriving to celebrate the first gallery where nobody gets the context, she watches a staff 'engagement guide' deliver an unscripted spoken talk to a cluster of a dozen visitors — the label didn't die, it went oral, and the flat field she came to praise has a hierarchy again, rebuilt in a channel that doesn't include her.
cross_cite: The position that the death of the wall label costs nothing and the companion app is pure gain — since the printed label was never legible to a blind visitor anyway and a screen-readable app is the first label she could ever read — treats the room's acoustic and digital layers as the real political territory, when the question is precisely whether a room that trusts speech and screens over print has demoted anyone, and whom.
opening_scene: A wall label is the only voice in a museum that speaks my language by default.
resisting_example: Christine Sun Kim — deaf, an artist whose whole practice runs on text — plastered Manchester's buildings in 2021 with giant hand-drawn captions like '[the sound of no wall text]' precisely because she considers the institutional label a flattened, condescending form of access, not its guarantee; she is not mourning the wall label, she is the one holding the crowbar.
seed_sentence: A wall label is the only voice in a museum that speaks my language by default.
